One of the biggest mistakes investors make is assuming a stock near its lows is “cheap” while a stock near its highs is “expensive.”

William O’Neil explained this perfectly:

“What seems too high usually goes higher and what seems too low usually goes lower.”

There’s a reason stocks near 52-week highs deserve attention. Consistently making new highs can signal strong relative strength, institutional accumulation, improving fundamentals and demand overwhelming supply.

Meanwhile, stocks making new lows often look attractive simply because they’re down 40%, 50% or 70%. But being down 70% doesn’t automatically make something cheap. Cheap can always get cheaper when the fundamentals and technical structure are deteriorating.

Another misconception is that a new ATH means the opportunity is already gone. A stock can spend months building a massive base, digesting its previous move and allowing earnings to catch up. When it finally breaks into new highs, that can actually be the beginning of the next major move, not the end.

Many of the greatest winners didn’t make one new high and stop. They made new highs, consolidated, built another base and continued higher as earnings and institutional demand followed.

None of this means blindly buying every stock at ATHs. There’s a massive difference between chasing an extended stock and buying a strong company breaking out of a proper base with explosive earnings growth + institutional accumulation.

New highs ≠ automatically expensive.
New lows ≠ automatically cheap.

Sometimes stocks make new highs for a reason, and sometimes they make new lows for a reason.

The market has a habit of rewarding strength and punishing weakness far longer than most people expect.

O'Neil's criterion: on the breakout, volume at least 40 to 50% above normal.
 In this study: 1.4x the 50-day average or more, on breakout day or one of the five sessions before.
 What I found: 72% of the big moves had it. On the day itself, 56% traded 1.4x or more, and 13% traded 5x or more. An ordinary day reaches 1.4x about 1/6 days. A day with a new 52-week high, about one in four.

M, market direction
 O'Neil's criterion: read the indexes every day. Distribution days mark the tops, and a follow-through day confirms the new uptrend.
 In this study: a simple stand-in, QQQ above its 50-day average.
 What I found: 85% of the big moves broke out with QQQ above its 50-day. So did 84% of all breakouts.

The stock's own 50-day On breakout day every one of the 4,048 moves was above its own 50-day, which follows from a new 52-week high. At month-end, stocks above their 50-day hit a big move about as often as the pool, and were down 30% or more six months later less often: 7.6% against 9.8%.

The yes/no split hides something, though. Stocks more than 20% above their 50-day, and stocks more than 20% below it, both hit a big move about four times as often as the rest. The ones sitting right on it hit least often.

So heavy volume was about twice as common in the big moves as on other new-high days. Being above the 50-day was there for every one of them, and for most of the rest too.

(Dow Jones) -- Rivian Automotive delivered and produced more vehicles in the third quarter, the first full quarter to include its newest model, the R2 SUV.
The electric vehicle maker said Friday it delivered 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter, up from 13,201 in the year-ago period. Analysts polled by FactSet expected 18,000 deliveries.
Rivian produced 19,751 vehicles at its manufacturing facility in Normal, Ill., over the same period, compared with 10,720 in the prior year.
Rivian said the results are in line with its outlook, and backed its forecast for 65,000 to 70,000 deliveries this year. The company had raised its outlook in July, weeks after its debuted the R2 in June.
The R2 is cheaper than previous Rivian models, and the company is planning to offer R2 variants that are priced even lower later this year and next year. Rivian executives have said they expect the more affordable electric SUV could help make the brand a mainstream success.

A small mindset trick that genuinely improved my trading: remove resistance levels from your charts and keep your support levels.

Sounds weird, right? But I've found that constantly identifying potential resistance creates expectations about where price should stop, often leading me to trim too early, hesitate or overthink perfectly healthy trends.

I'd rather focus on where my thesis would be invalidated, manage risk around structure and remain open-minded about how far a leader can actually go.

Stop trying to predict where the upside ends. Focus on knowing where you're wrong.

Sometimes, removing a few lines from your charts removes a whole lot of psychological barriers. 😉
